present.name: Present-tense forms
present.about: The verb changes with who does it: je parle (I speak), tu parles (you speak), il or elle parle (he or she speaks), nous parlons (we speak), vous parlez (you speak), ils or elles parlent (they speak).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb changes with who does it: je mange, tu manges, il mange, nous mangeons (I eat, you eat, he eats, we eat).

gender.name: Gender and agreement
gender.about: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and le or la, un or une and the adjectives with it match it: un petit chat, une petite maison.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is a le word or a la word, and un or une and its adjectives match: le téléphone, la table, un café, une clé.

adjective-after.name: Adjective position
adjective-after.about: Many adjectives follow the noun: la porte ouverte. Common adjectives such as petit, grand, bon, beau, jeune and nouveau usually come before it. The adjective also matches the noun: un petit livre, une petite tasse.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Changed in revision 7.

adjective-after.short: Petit goes before the noun: un petit livre, une petite tasse. Many other adjectives follow it: la porte ouverte.

negation.name: ne … pas around the verb
negation.about: ne goes before the verb and pas after it: Je ne sais pas (I not know not); in the passé composé they go around avoir or être (Je n'ai pas mangé), and everyday speech often drops ne.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

negation.short: ne goes before the verb and pas after it: Je ne bois pas de café (I don't drink coffee); before a vowel ne is n': Il n'est pas ici.

question.name: Questions
question.about: Ask by raising your voice at the end, or start with est-ce que (is it that). After a question word, the verb can come before the subject: À quelle heure part le train (at what hour leaves the train).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: Raise your voice at the end to ask, or start with a question word: Tu viens? (you come?), Où est la voiture? (where is the car?)

object-pronoun.name: Pronouns before the verb
object-pronoun.about: le, la and les (him, her, it, them), me, te and lui (to him or her) go before the verb, or before the infinitive of a second verb: Je le vois (I it see), Je veux te voir (I want you see).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

object-pronoun.short: le, la, les, me, te and lui go before the verb: Je le vois (I it see: I see it).

perfect.name: Completed events, including could and had to
perfect.about: Avoir plus a past participle describes a completed event. With pouvoir, devoir and vouloir, use pu, dû and voulu, followed by an infinitive: On a pu ouvrir la porte; J'ai dû partir; Mon fils n'a pas voulu manger (he refused to eat). The auxiliary changes with the subject; the following verb stays in the infinitive.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Changed in revision 6.

perfect.short: Avoir plus a past participle tells what happened: J'ai mangé, for I ate or I've eaten. After pu, dû or voulu an infinitive follows: J'ai dû partir.

etre-perfect.name: passé composé with être
etre-perfect.about: A small group of verbs, including aller, venir, partir, arriver and rester, use être instead, and the participle matches the subject: Elle est partie (she is gone: she left).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

etre-perfect.short: A few verbs like aller, venir and partir use être, and the participle matches: Elle est partie (she is gone: she left).

aller.name: aller + infinitive: going to
aller.about: Je vais, tu vas, il va and an infinitive say what's going to happen, with no word for to: Je vais manger (I go eat).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

aller.short: aller and an infinitive say what's going to happen, with no word for to: Je vais manger (I go eat: I'm going to eat).

modal.name: Verb + infinitive
modal.about: After vouloir, pouvoir, devoir and aimer, the next verb stays in the infinitive, with no word for to: Je veux partir (I want leave).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After vouloir, pouvoir and devoir the next verb stays in its basic form, with no word for to: Je veux manger (I want eat).

partitive.name: du, de la, des: some
partitive.about: du or de la is some of something you don't count (du café) and des is some of things you do (des tomates); after a negative verb they usually become de (pas de café), while aimer in a general sense takes le, la or les (j'aime le café).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

partitive.chip: du, de la, de l': some
partitive.short: du goes with le words, de la with la words and de l' before a vowel, often with no English word: Je bois du café, de l'eau (I drink coffee, water).

contraction.name: au and du
contraction.about: à le becomes au and de le becomes du: au marché (to-the market), du travail (from-the work). à la and de la stay as they are.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

contraction.short: à le becomes au and de le becomes du: au marché (to the market), le livre du professeur (the teacher's book).

de.name: de: of
de.about: French joins nouns with de where English uses 's: la voiture de mon père (the car of my father).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

de.short: French joins nouns with de where English uses 's: le livre de ma mère (the book of my mother: my mother's book).

il-y-a.name: il y a: there is, there are
il-y-a.about: il y a says both there is and there are: Il y a un problème (it there has a problem).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover there are too in revision 5 (the director, 2026-11-09).

il-y-a.chip: il y a: there is or are
il-y-a.short: il y a says both there is and there are: Il y a un problème (there's a problem).

avoir.name: avoir: I have hunger
avoir.about: Where English says I'm hungry, thirsty or twenty, French says I have: J'ai faim (I have hunger), J'ai vingt ans (I have twenty years).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover need, age, pain and the rest too in revision 5 (the director, 2026-11-09).

avoir.short: Where English says I'm hungry or I'm twenty, French says I have: J'ai faim (I have hunger), J'ai vingt ans.

reflexive.name: Reflexive verbs
reflexive.about: With reflexive verbs, me, te, se or nous goes before the verb and points back to whoever does it, or means each other: Je me lève (I myself raise: I get up), On se voit (one each other sees: we meet).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

reflexive.short: me, te, se or nous goes before the verb and points back to whoever does it: Je me lève (I myself raise: I get up).

y-en.name: Y and en: places, things and amounts
y-en.about: Y can stand for a place or an à complement referring to a thing: Je pense à ce plan; j'y pense. En can stand for a de complement: Je parle de ce plan; j'en parle. In Qu'est-ce que tu en penses?, en goes with penser de. For a person, these examples use penser à elle and parler de lui. With a quantity, keep the amount: J'en ai deux.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Changed in revision 6.

y-en.short: Y stands for a place or à + a thing: j'y vais, j'y pense. En stands for de + a thing or an amount: j'en parle, j'en ai deux.

il-fait.name: il fait: the weather
il-fait.about: French talks about the weather with faire: Il fait beau (it makes beautiful: it's nice out), Il fait froid (it's cold).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

il-fait.short: French talks about the weather with faire: Il fait beau (it makes beautiful: it's nice out), Il fait froid (it's cold).

on.name: on: we
on.about: In everyday French, on (one) usually means we, with the verb's il form: On y va (one there goes: let's go).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

on.short: In everyday French on (one) usually means we, with the verb's il form: On y va (one there goes: let's go).

possessive.name: mon, ma, ton, ta: my and your
possessive.about: mon (my) and ton (your) go before a le word, ma and ta before a la word; before a la word that starts with a vowel it's mon and ton again: mon livre, ma clé, mon amie. With a plural noun it's mes and tes.

source.note: Added with the French lessons, open to correction.

possessive.short: mon and ton go before a le word, ma and ta before a la word: mon téléphone, ma clé (my phone, my key).

demonstrative.name: ce, cet, cette: this and that
demonstrative.about: ce goes before a le word, cet before a le word that starts with a vowel, and cette before a la word, for this or that: ce livre, cet hôtel, cette clé. With a plural noun it's ces.

source.note: Added with the French lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: ce goes before a le word and cette before a la word, for this or that: ce livre, cette clé; cet before a le word that starts with a vowel.

vous.name: vous: polite you
vous.about: vous is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, and you to more than one person; its verb usually ends in -ez (vous êtes is the big exception): Vous savez où c'est? (you know where it is?), C'est pour vous (it's for you).

source.note: Added with the French lessons, open to correction.

vous.short: vous is the polite you, and you to more than one; its verb usually ends in -ez (vous êtes is the big exception): Vous savez? Vous voulez un café?

elision.name: Short words joined by an apostrophe
elision.about: Before a vowel sound, je, le, la, ne and de can lose their final vowel: j'ai, l'eau, n'est, d'eau. This is elision. Mute h also allows it; aspirate h blocks it. Learn which kind of h a word has.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

elision.short: Before a vowel, je becomes j', le and la become l', ne becomes n' and de becomes d': j'ai, l'eau, n'est, d'eau.

question-word.name: Question words
question-word.about: qui asks who, que or quoi what, où where, comment how, quand when and combien how much. Qu'est-ce que introduces a what question; quoi can go at the end. A question word does not require inversion: Comment je peux aider? keeps je before peux.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

question-word.short: qui = who; que or quoi = what; où = where; comment = how; quand = when; combien = how much. Qu'est-ce que starts a what question; quoi can come at the end.

tonic-pronoun.name: toi after a preposition
tonic-pronoun.about: Use toi, not tu, after a preposition: avec toi (with you), chez toi (at your place). tu is the subject form, as in Tu viens. These are two forms for the same person.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Short name made to cover chez, entre and moi too in revision 5 (the director, 2026-11-09).

tonic-pronoun.short: After avec or chez, use toi: Je veux être avec toi (I want to be with you). tu is the subject form.

imperative.name: Giving an instruction
imperative.about: To give an instruction, use the command form without tu or vous: Appelle ton père; Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plaît. Appelle addresses one familiar person; appelez is polite or plural. Keep that choice in the rest of the sentence.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

imperative.short: An instruction has no subject pronoun: Appelle ton père. Use Appelez with polite or plural you: Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plaît.

conditional.name: Would, could and polite requests
conditional.about: The conditional uses the future stem with -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. It expresses would or could, and softens requests. Vouloir gives voudrais; être gives serais; pouvoir gives pourrais and pourrions. An imagined condition can use si plus the imperfect followed by a conditional outcome: Si j'avais le temps, je pourrais t'aider.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 5.

conditional.short: Use the future stem with imperfect endings for the conditional. Si plus the imperfect can introduce an imagined condition: Si j'avais le temps, je pourrais t'aider.

time.name: Telling the time
time.about: Use il est to tell the time and à for the time of an event. Deux heures et demie is half past two; trois heures et quart is a quarter past three; quatre heures moins le quart is a quarter to four. Write demie after heures, but demi after midi. A time phrase can come first or last.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Short name made to cover other times and days too in revision 5 (the director, 2026-11-09). Changed in revision 7.

time.short: Il est deux heures et demie: half past two. Et quart adds a quarter; moins le quart subtracts one. Midi et demi: half past noon.

infinitive-link.name: Links before an infinitive
infinitive-link.about: Learn à or de with the verb or expression: difficile à comprendre, oublier de t'appeler, avant de rentrer. Pour plus an infinitive expresses purpose. The linked verb stays in the infinitive, and its object pronoun goes before it.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 6.

infinitive-link.short: Use the link each expression requires: difficile à comprendre; oublier de t'appeler; avant de rentrer. Pour introduces a purpose.

indirect-question.name: A question inside a sentence
indirect-question.about: ce que introduces what someone says or does inside another sentence: Vous comprenez ce que je dis? Keep je before dis. Do not put the direct-question phrase qu'est-ce que in that position.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

indirect-question.short: Inside a sentence, ce que can mean what: Vous comprenez ce que je dis? (do you understand what I'm saying?). je stays before dis.

cest-il-est.name: c'est and il est
cest-il-est.about: C'est un mot difficile identifies something with a noun phrase. Il est difficile describes a masculine thing already identified, such as a word or book. C'est difficile can also describe a whole situation or task.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

cest-il-est.short: Use c'est to identify: C'est un mot difficile. Use il est to describe a known masculine thing: Il est difficile. C'est difficile can describe a situation.

because.name: Giving a reason: car and parce que
because.about: car and parce que both give a reason, with the subject before its verb. car usually follows the statement it explains and is more common in writing; parce que is the usual everyday because.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

because.short: car and parce que give a reason. Keep the subject before its verb: Je reste au lit, car je veux dormir.

que-clause.name: Saying what you think
que-clause.about: After je pense, que introduces a statement with its own subject and verb: Je pense que nous pouvons manger ici. Before il or elle, que becomes qu': qu'il, qu'elle. These affirmative statements use the indicative.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

que-clause.short: Keep que after pense: Je pense que nous pouvons manger ici. Before il or elle, use qu': Je pense qu'il est à la maison.

plural.name: More than one
plural.about: A regular noun usually adds written -s for more than one: deux heures, trois heures. That final -s is normally silent. Here the number already tells you that there is more than one.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

plural.short: For more than one hour, write heures: à deux heures, à trois heures. The final -s is normally silent.

verb-preposition.name: The verb's own link
verb-preposition.about: Learn the French construction with the verb: écouter la musique has no à, and attendre le médecin has no pour. Other verbs have a link: penser à une tasse de café, parler de ce film.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

verb-preposition.short: écouter la musique and attendre le médecin take the object directly. penser à and parler de keep their own link; English may use a different one.

negative-words.name: Never, nothing and only
negative-words.about: Ne ... jamais means never; ne ... rien means nothing or not anything. In these ordinary negatives, do not add pas. Ne ... que is a restriction meaning only: Je n'ai que deux messages. Que comes before the restricted part: Nous ne sommes en contact qu'au travail. Ne ... pas que means not only.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 7.

negative-words.short: Ne ... jamais says never, ne ... rien says nothing, and ne ... que says only: Je n'ai que deux messages.

subjunctive.name: The subjunctive after certain expressions
subjunctive.about: Jusqu'à ce que, avant que, il faut que, vouloir que and c'est normal que take the subjunctive in these examples. Some forms look like the ordinary present; soit and parte show different forms. Affirmative espérer normally takes the indicative. Pour que introduces a purpose and also takes the subjunctive: pour que nous puissions jouer.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

subjunctive.short: Some expressions with que take the subjunctive: il faut que j'aie, jusqu'à ce que tu arrives, pour que nous puissions jouer.

participle-agreement.name: Which word the participle agrees with
participle-agreement.about: With s'asseoir and the être past forms shown here, the participle agrees with the subject. In the passive it also agrees with the subject. With avoir, a preceding direct object controls agreement: Cette histoire m'a touché for a male speaker, touchée for a female speaker. Other pronominal constructions need their own rules.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 6.

participle-agreement.short: Match the relevant noun or pronoun: Elle est allée; La porte a été ouverte. With avoir, a preceding direct object matters: Cette histoire m'a touché.

object-order.name: Two object pronouns together
object-order.about: In the combinations shown here, me or te comes before le or la, before the verb: Je te le donne. In a positive command the order changes: Donne-le-moi. In a negative command, use the order before the verb again: Ne me le donne pas. The positive command joins the verb and pronouns with hyphens.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

object-order.short: Before the verb: Je te le donne. Positive command: Donne-le-moi. Negative command: Ne me le donne pas.

comparative.name: More, less, as much and better
comparative.about: Use plus, moins or aussi before an adjective or adverb and que before the comparison. Bon uses meilleur, which agrees with its noun; bien uses the unchanging mieux. Plus tôt and plus tard compare times. Plutôt can mark a preference, as in Je voudrais plutôt du thé.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 6.

comparative.short: Plus grande que, moins grande que and aussi grande que compare size. Bon becomes meilleur; bien becomes mieux.

imperfect.name: Past situations and completed events
imperfect.about: The imperfect presents a past situation, habit or ongoing action; the passé composé presents a completed event. Most imperfect stems come from the present nous form without -ons; être uses ét-. Add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Nous travaillions dans cette maison quand tu as appelé puts the ongoing work in the imperfect and the call in the passé composé.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

imperfect.short: The imperfect describes a past situation or habit; the passé composé presents a completed event: Nous travaillions dans cette maison quand tu as appelé.

if-when.name: If, when and as if
if-when.about: Si introduces a condition. Use si plus the present for a possible condition, or si plus the imperfect with a conditional outcome for an imagined situation. Quand locates an event; when the event is future, French uses a future form after quand. Comme si introduces an imagined comparison, here with the imperfect.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

if-when.short: Si tu veux, tu peux rester. Si j'avais le temps, je pourrais t'appeler. For future time, use quand je serai, even though English says when I am.

particles.name: Small words that set the tone
particles.about: In these uses, mais expresses surprise, donc encourages, quand même marks a contrast with expectations, and bien softens aimer. Compare Mais pourquoi tu as peur? (why on earth are you scared?), Appelle donc ton père (go on, call your dad) and J'aime bien ce café (I quite like this coffee). These are context-dependent uses; mais also means but and donc can mean so.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

particles.short: Mais pourquoi adds surprise; Appelle donc encourages; quand même means anyway or after all here; aimer bien means like, with a moderate tone.

future.name: The simple future
future.about: The simple future joins a future stem to -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. For many verbs the stem is the infinitive; an -re infinitive loses its final e. Some stems change: appeler uses appeller-. Je t'appellerai demain makes a promise; Nous resterons probablement à la maison demain makes a prediction. Aller plus an infinitive also expresses a future plan.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

future.short: Add a future ending to the future stem: Je t'appellerai demain; Nous resterons probablement à la maison demain.

relative.name: Who, that, about which and where
relative.about: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Qui is the subject of its clause; que is its direct object. Dont supplies a de complement, as in le mot dont je parle. Où links a place to what happens there. Keep the familiar la façon dont for the way something is done.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

relative.short: Qui does the action; que receives it; dont supplies de; où links a place to its description.

duration.name: Ongoing time and measured duration
duration.about: Depuis with the present describes a situation continuing now. A bare quantity can measure time spent: travailler six heures. Pendant gives the duration of an event or repeated situation. Par jour gives a daily amount. Keep depuis for an ongoing situation extending back to a starting point.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

duration.short: Depuis with the present extends a situation back in time. A quantity of hours can also measure the time spent on an action.

progressive.name: An action in progress
progressive.about: The present often translates am doing. Être en train de plus an infinitive explicitly presents an action as in progress now. Conjugate être for the subject and keep the following verb in its infinitive. It is useful when the ongoing action matters, not necessary for every present action.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

progressive.short: Être en train de plus an infinitive stresses an action in progress: Je suis en train de travailler.

noun-pronoun.name: This one and that one
noun-pronoun.about: Celui-ci and celui-là replace a masculine singular noun already understood: celui-ci is this one, celui-là that one. With téléphone understood, Tu veux vendre celui-là? asks about that phone without repeating téléphone. Celle-ci and celle-là replace a feminine singular noun: cette chambre, celle-là.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

noun-pronoun.short: Use celui-ci or celui-là for a masculine noun; celle-ci or celle-là for a feminine noun.

gerund.name: Two actions at the same time
gerund.about: En plus a present participle links a simultaneous action to the main action. The same person or people perform both: Je mange en lisant. The -ant form does not change with gender or number. Learn each -ant form with its verb: lisant (lire), mangeant (manger), marchant (marcher).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

gerund.short: En plus an -ant form gives a second action with the same subject: Je mange en lisant.

past-perfect.name: Before another past moment
past-perfect.about: The plus-que-parfait uses the imperfect of avoir or être with a past participle to place an event before a past reference point. The reference point can be supplied by the conversation. Keep the auxiliary and participle agreement used for that verb in the passé composé.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

past-perfect.short: Use imperfect avoir or être plus a past participle for an earlier past event: J'avais déjà mangé; il était déjà rentré.

passive.name: What is done: the passive
passive.about: Use être with a past participle to describe what is done to the subject. The participle agrees with that subject in gender and number. Par can introduce the person who performs the action. In the passé composé, être becomes a été: La porte a été ouverte. Everyday French often uses on with an active verb when the person doing the action is not specified.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

passive.short: The subject receives the action: Ce livre est lu par mon père. Match the participle to it: La porte a été ouverte.

superlative.name: The most, the least and the best
superlative.about: Use a definite article with plus or moins to pick out an extreme within a group. In la maison la plus grande, both la and grande agree with maison. The superlative of bon uses meilleur: le meilleur choix.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

superlative.short: La maison la plus grande is the biggest house; le meilleur choix is the best choice.

reported-speech.name: Reporting someone's words
reported-speech.about: Que introduces a reported statement; si introduces a reported yes/no question. After a past reporting verb, the present often shifts to the imperfect, a completed past to the past perfect, and a future to the conditional. The time viewpoint matters: a present can stay present if it is still true. A reported question keeps subject before verb, without est-ce que.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 7.

reported-speech.short: Il a dit qu'il était malade reports a statement; Elle a demandé si tu venais reports a yes/no question.

past-conditional.name: Would have and should have
past-conditional.about: Use conditional avoir or être with a past participle for an imagined past outcome. J'aurais dû t'appeler expresses a missed obligation or regret. A condition about an unreal past uses si with the past perfect: Si j'avais su, je serais venu. Keep the verb's usual auxiliary and agreement rules.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 7.

past-conditional.short: J'aurais dû t'appeler means I should have called you; je serais venu means I would have come.

causative.name: Having something done
causative.about: Faire plus an infinitive can describe arranging for an action to be done: Je dois faire examiner ma jambe. Faire carries the tense. In the compound past, fait stays unchanged before the infinitive, even with a preceding feminine direct object: la jambe que j'ai fait examiner.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 7.

causative.short: J'ai fait examiner ma jambe means I had my leg examined. Keep examiner in the infinitive and fait unchanged.

recent-past.name: Something just happened
recent-past.about: Use venir de plus an infinitive for something that just happened: Je viens de rentrer. With venir in the imperfect, the event had just happened at a past moment: Il venait de partir quand j'ai appelé.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 7.

recent-past.short: Je viens de rentrer means I just got home; Il venait de partir means he had just left.
